one_liner: Pure-Rust sparse LDL^T/LU/KLU direct solver; solve phase 2.3-3.3x faster than MKL PARDISO, factorization usually slower.
what_it_does: A sparse direct solver for real and complex matrices (f32, f64, Complex<f32>, Complex<f64>) that needs no BLAS, LAPACK or MKL. It has three paths: Bunch-Kaufman LDL^T for symmetric and complex-symmetric matrices, threshold-pivoting LU for unsymmetric ones, and KLU (block triangular form plus per-block Gilbert-Peierls LU) for circuit matrices. The API is phased like PARDISO: `XSymbolic::analyze` once per pattern, `factor` for each new set of values, then `solve`, `solve_many`, `solve_transpose` or `solve_refined`; the KLU path adds a numeric-only `refactor`. Every factor can also precondition the built-in GMRES, block GMRES, COCG and COCR solvers, and Python bindings (`rslab.spsolve`, `rslab.lu`, `rslab.analyze`) accept SciPy sparse matrices.
how_it_is_fast: LDL^T and LU are left-looking and supernodal, run in parallel over the elimination tree in a scoped rayon pool, and do their dense updates with the pure-Rust `gemm` crate (runtime AVX2/AVX-512 dispatch). Several fill-reducing orderings (AMD, AMF, RCM, parallel nested dissection) are tried and raced on the exact fill each produces, with MC64-style matching and scaling. The solve-phase advantage comes from supernodal, tree-parallel triangular solves over the factor's panels. The KLU path factors independent BTF blocks in parallel and refactors without a new pivot search.
when_to_use: Many solves per factorization (multiple right-hand sides, iterative refinement, Krylov preconditioning), where the solve phase at 0.30-0.43x PARDISO's time dominates.
Method-of-moments near-field systems (complex): the one class where factor (0.95), refactor (0.90) and one-shot (0.74) time also beat PARDISO.
Rust or Python projects that want a PARDISO-style solver without an MKL, BLAS or LAPACK dependency, or that need factors bit-identical across thread counts.
Embedded or scheduled solves that must check memory before factoring: `memory_plan` and `estimate_memory` predict the heap peak from the analysis alone.
Circuit-simulation sweeps on a fixed pattern through KLU `refactor`, or GMRES/COCG with a factor of a nearby matrix that never fails thanks to static pivoting.
when_not_to_use: Workloads dominated by factorization or one-shot solves on FEM curl-curl (factor 1.35x PARDISO's time), power-grid (3.97x) or circuit (4.76x) matrices, where PARDISO is faster.
Medium-size circuit matrices with frequent refactorization: open issue #88 reports KLU refactor 3-8x behind PARDISO.

Large complex-symmetric factorizations under memory pressure (#87: peak memory 2.3x PARDISO's), or x86 machines with many cores (#82: factorization scales poorly; #83: symbolic analysis takes 2.8x PARDISO's time).

Saddle-point matrices with zero diagonals on the LU path with the default `lu_matching = true`. Issue #74 reports 154-408 floored pivots and 5e-5 relative accuracy on a complex EM saddle matrix, vs 1e-12 with matching off.
C or C++ codebases (no C API; FFI exists only in the Python bindings), or teams that need a mature solver: 12 stars, and 31 PyPI releases between 2026-06-29 and 2026-09-29.

integration.dependencies: rayon, gemm 0.19, num-complex, serde/serde_json, plus in-workspace ordering crates (AMD, AMF, METIS-style nested dissection); optional ureq/flate2/tar (feature matgen-download) and sysinfo (feature tuning); Python wheels need numpy>=1.21 and scipy>=1.7
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition on current stable (rust-toolchain.toml tracks stable; no rust-version/MSRV declared); Python >= 3.9 for the bindings
integration.platforms: pure Rust (runtime AVX2/AVX-512 dispatch on x86, wasm32 clock shim in source); PyPI abi3 wheels for Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (manylinux_2_28), macOS x86-64 and arm64, and Windows x86-64
integration.thread_safety: Each factorization runs in its own scoped pool. Threads::Auto caps workers at 4 'so concurrent solves coexist', Threads::Ambient runs on the caller's rayon pool, and a caller-owned flag can interrupt a running factorization. Sharing one factor object across threads is not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same phases (analyze, factor, solve) and matrix classes as PARDISO mtype 2, 6, 11 and 13, but a Rust/Python API, not the pardiso() C/Fortran interface

gotchas: The crates.io name `rslab` belongs to an unrelated slab-allocator crate (versions 0.1-0.2 from 2022). Depend on the git tag as the README shows; `cargo add rslab` pulls the wrong crate.
The default Threads::Auto caps workers at 4. The README benchmark passed 12 threads explicitly, so pass `threads=0` (all cores) or `'auto'` to match it.
The dense kernels allocate per product. The docs recommend a caching global allocator such as mimalloc, especially on Windows.
Licensing: the code is MIT and forked from feral (MIT), with Hungarian/MC64 routines translated from SPRAL (BSD-3-Clause). Releases 0.20.0-0.23.0 contained METIS-derived Apache-2.0 code (see NOTICE).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against GSS (trial binaries only, also benchmarked against PARDISO), pick RSLAB when you need MIT source and fast repeated solves. Pick CKTSO for C/C++ circuit simulators that care most about parallel factorization speed against KLU, and BaSpaCho for SPD Cholesky in C++. RSLAB covers indefinite, complex-symmetric and unsymmetric matrices in Rust or Python.
verified_claims_summary: The README table gives wall time relative to MKL PARDISO (pardisoinit defaults, taking the faster of classic and two-level factorization) on 28 non-public production systems at 12 threads, as a geomean per class. Solve time is 0.30-0.43 of PARDISO's (2.3-3.3x faster), while factorization is 0.95-4.76 and one-shot 0.74-1.12, so RSLAB is ahead end-to-end only on MoM near field. Both solvers are timed from the same Python harness (benches/pardiso_corpus.py), PARDISO through ctypes against pip-installed MKL; CPU model, Rust version and flags are not stated.
status_note: Very active but young: 624 commits, v1.1.0 released 2026-09-29, 12 stars, one listed author, and open performance issues against PARDISO (#82, #83, #87, #88). MIT-licensed, installed from git or from PyPI wheels.
